objections.argument: This is asserted as the 'worst outcome' combination but the claim never establishes that the alternative (rebuild deferred to a year with slack) actually arrives. If slack never materializes in future years either, delaying the rebuild indefinitely under this logic just relocates the same risk forward while the pipeline keeps degrading — the claim treats the current year's constraint as uniquely bad rather than checking whether it is representative of every future year.

The claim generalizes from 'three-year-old ingestion pipelines' as a class to this specific pipeline without any profiling data cited in the sheet itself. 'Almost always' hotspot-dominated is an empirical claim about a reference class that may not include pipelines already hitting genuine architectural ceilings, and the sheet's own assumptions section admits profiling may not have happened — so claim 2 is doing load-bearing work on a premise the author flags elsewhere as unverified.

This draws a clean latency-versus-throughput distinction that doesn't hold in practice: streaming architectures frequently improve throughput and cost too, via continuous small-batch processing that avoids large periodic scan costs and enables incremental/partial reprocessing instead of full reruns. Framing it as strictly 'the wrong axis' overstates a real but partial distinction into a categorical one.

This proves too much: by the same logic, any refactor that touches the same code paths also risks losing tacit correctness handling that isn't documented anywhere, since refactoring under 'no slack' with the same team is exactly the condition claim 1 says produces the worst outcomes. The claim treats rediscovery risk as unique to rebuilds when it's a function of documentation quality, not architecture choice.

Asserting the decoupling 'costs far less than the rebuild does' is a bare cost comparison with no basis given — building and maintaining a decoupled write path is itself ongoing engineering investment that could stall, be abandoned, or accumulate its own tech debt, and the claim doesn't address the risk that this 'small fixed slice' quietly grows under the same zero-slack roadmap pressure claim 1 warns about.

This claim treats 'no slack' as fixed and unquestionable, but it's a scheduling decision, not a physical constraint — the asymmetric downside risk it describes is really an argument against attempting the rebuild without first negotiating slack, not an argument against rebuilding per se. The claim smuggles in a false binary between 'rebuild now under current constraints' and 'refactor,' skipping the option of renegotiating scope before deciding architecture.

Listing 'parallelization, caching, storage tuning' as generally available levers assumes these haven't already been tried in a three-year-old pipeline that is presumably not brand new to optimization efforts — mature pipelines often have already captured the easy tuning wins, and the claim gives no basis for assuming untapped headroom exists here specifically.

This claim frames operational complexity and team-expertise mismatch as reasons against streaming, but it never engages with the inverse risk: staying on a paradigm the team already knows may be exactly why the three-year-old bottleneck has persisted uncorrected. Familiarity is treated as a pure asset when it's equally plausible the team's existing expertise is capped at what batch tooling can deliver.

This explicitly invokes 'sunk cost' while arguing for continuity with the existing system — that is the sunk cost fallacy pointed at itself: preserving the current storage format because switching it is costly is precisely the reasoning pattern the term is used to warn against, not a valid reason on its own to avoid the switch.

'Preserves the ability to reverse decisions' is asserted as a general property of refactoring, but nothing in the sheet establishes that the specific refactor path chosen would remain reversible — incremental refactors can themselves accrete irreversible dependencies (schema migrations, downstream consumer coupling) just as a rebuild can, and the claim treats reversibility as intrinsic to the refactor strategy rather than something that must be separately engineered and could be lost just as easily.
